title: Recollecting the Buddha
hookLine: a deadline, a shortcut nobody would notice, and an old practice about who's in the room

lines: ITI PI SO: THUS INDEED IS HE.
cards: Plenty of people act differently when a coach, a grandparent or a hero walks into the room. Shoulders go back. The phone goes away.

A joke gets edited. So, yesterday's question: who would you want watching when nobody's watching? Buddhaghosa has an answer, and it comes with a practice: calling to mind the Buddha's qualities, buddhanussati.
The words are old ones: iti pi so bhagava. Thus indeed is he, the Blessed One: worthy, fully awake, perfect in knowledge and conduct, and on down the list.

teach.h: AS IF IN THE TEACHER'S PRESENCE.
teach.b: Here's what the manual says happens to someone who keeps at it. He comes to feel as if he's living in the Teacher's presence. His body, Buddhaghosa says, becomes worthy of honor, like a shrine room.
And the part that matters on an ordinary afternoon: when a chance to do wrong comes along, he feels conscience and shame as clearly as if he were standing face to face with the Teacher.
Notice what that is, and what it isn't.

teach.h: NOT A CAMERA: A MENTOR'S VOICE.
teach.b: It isn't a camera, or fear of being caught; there's no punishment in the passage. It's closer to the way a good mentor stays in your head long after the lesson.
You hear the voice, and you'd rather be the person they saw in you. The manual adds an honest limit, too.

teach.h: TO THE EDGE OF DEEP CALM.
teach.b: Because the Buddha's qualities are so many and so deep, this recollection brings the mind to the edge of deep concentration, not all the way in. It's a practice for a steady, good-hearted day more than for a trance.
So who would you want watching? Someone whose qualities you can name, one by one. That's why the old formula names them.

how: Many Theravada Buddhists chant the recollection of the Buddha, iti pi so bhagava, in daily and temple chanting; as a meditation it is practiced by calling the qualities to mind one at a time, as Visuddhimagga 7 describes.

o: retelling the stories of the Buddha's past lives
calling the Buddha's qualities to mind, one by one
praying to the Buddha to grant a wish or a favor

games.q: the recollection, piece by piece — tap the pairs.
p: conscience as clear as in his presence

s: recollecting the Buddha works like a security camera: fear of getting caught
the passage has no punishment in it. it's conscience, as if face to face with a teacher.
Buddhaghosa says this recollection brings the mind to the edge of deep concentration, not all the way in
the Buddha's qualities are many and deep, so the mind doesn't settle fully into one.
iti pi so names the Buddha's qualities one by one
worthy, fully awake, perfect in knowledge and conduct, and on down the list.

games.q: at your part-time job the manager's out, and a coworker says to write down a later clock-out time. you think of your grandmother. which reading of today's teaching fits?
o: you're scared she'll find out somehow and be angry with you.
you'd rather be the person she sees in you, so you don't.
you picture her, feel a little guilty, and then do it anyway.
games.why: the manual's picture is conscience as clear as being face to face with someone good. not fear of being caught: wanting to be who they see.

practice: If you'd like, say the opening line slowly, out loud or under your breath: iti pi so bhagava, thus indeed is he, the Blessed One. Then name a few qualities, one at a time: worthy, fully awake, perfect in knowledge and conduct.
After each, pause and let that quality stand there, the way a mentor's face would.

wordCard.voice: Buddhanussati: recollecting the Buddha. Calling his qualities to mind, one by one, until it feels like being in his presence.

orig.note: Pali: recollection (anussati) of the Buddha. The first of the recollections in Visuddhimagga 7.

carryVoice: Your line: thus indeed is he. A face to keep in mind when nobody else is around. Day nineteen of forty.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 7 (recollection of the Buddha: the practitioner comes to feel as if living in the Master's presence; his body becomes worthy of veneration like a shrine room; when an opportunity for transgression arises, conscience and shame are as vivid as if face to face with the Master; because the special qualities are profound and many, the jhana reaches only access)
The recollection of the Buddha (iti pi so bhagava araham sammasambuddho vijjacaranasampanno …), as in AN 6.10 and SN 11.3
